summary: This proposed standard defines how to represent configuration data, state data, RPC parameters and notifications defined in YANG as JSON text. It gives the rules so that data modeled in YANG can be exchanged in a format familiar to web developers.

eli5.summary: If a form template describes a device's settings, you still need a way to write them down. This says how to write them in JSON, a simple text format that lots of programs already read.

subtitle: The rules for writing YANG-modeled configuration, state, RPC and notification data as JSON text.

tldr.problem: YANG 1.1 only defines an XML encoding for data trees, but other management protocols such as RESTCONF want to carry the same data as JSON.
tldr.mechanism: Each YANG data node becomes a JSON object member, named with an optional module prefix, and each YANG type maps to a specific JSON value form. The rules follow the I-JSON profile as closely as possible.
tldr.outcome: A JSON-encoded data tree can be mapped to XML and back, provided the YANG model is available. It remains a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting RFC listed.

today: RFC 7951 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why YANG Data Needs a JSON Encoding
sections.content:
The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241) uses XML to encode data in its Content Layer. Other management protocols might want a different encoding while still using YANG as the data modeling language. RESTCONF is the example the RFC gives: it supports both XML and JSON.

The YANG 1.1 specification (RFC 7950) defines only the XML encoding of data trees, meaning configuration data, state data, input and output parameters of RPC operations or actions, and notifications. This document defines rules for encoding the same data as JSON text (RFC 7159).

The top-level structure of JSON-encoded data is always assumed to be an object. The encoding rules are the same for every kind of data tree. Apart from anydata, all the rules also apply to YANG 1.0 (RFC 6020).
sections.eli5: There was already a way to write down a device's settings in one text format called XML. This RFC adds a second way, JSON, which many web programmers like better.

sections.title: Member Names and Namespaces
sections.content:
Every data node instance is a name/value pair in a JSON object. The name must be in one of two forms. The simple form is just the YANG identifier. The namespace-qualified form puts the module name and a colon in front of the identifier. If a node is defined in a submodule, the qualified name uses the main module's name.

A qualified name MUST be used for all members of the top-level JSON object, and whenever the data node and its parent are defined in different namespaces. In every other case the simple form MUST be used. The ABNF is member-name = [identifier ":"] identifier.

In the RFC's example, a container top in module example-foomod holds a leaf foo from the same module, so only the outer name is qualified. When another module, example-barmod, augments top with a leaf bar, that leaf is written example-barmod:bar because its parent comes from a different module.

Qualified names also appear inside values: identityref and instance-identifier values use the same form when a namespace must be stated.
sections.eli5: It is like writing a last name only when two kids in the room share a first name. If everyone belongs to the same family, the first name is enough.

sections.title: Encoding the Data Node Kinds
sections.content:
Character encoding MUST be UTF-8. Each kind of YANG data node has its own JSON shape:

  • leaf: a name/value pair; the value is a string, number, true or false, or the special array [null], depending on the type.
  • container: a name/object pair, with the child nodes as members of the object.
  • leaf-list: a name/array pair of scalar values, in the order required by the ordered-by property.
  • list: a name/array pair whose elements are objects. Unlike XML, the order of members inside a list entry is arbitrary, because JSON objects are unordered.
  • anydata: encoded like a container. Its content must be valid I-JSON, use valid member names, and any array must hold either only unique scalars or only objects.
  • anyxml: a name/value pair whose value must satisfy I-JSON constraints.

A JSON document MAY also contain members whose name starts with @. They are meant for metadata (RFC 7952), and their syntax is outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: A single setting is a label with a value, a group of settings is a box with labels inside, and a list is a row of such boxes. Each kind of thing has its own simple way to be written.

sections.title: Representing YANG Types as JSON Values
sections.content:
JSON values carry partial type information (number, string, boolean), and the encoding is defined so that this never conflicts with the YANG type of the leaf. The main rules:

  • int8, int16, int32, uint8, uint16 and uint32 are JSON numbers.
  • int64, uint64 and decimal64 are JSON strings holding the lexical form. A uint64 leaf foo is written "foo": "123".
  • boolean is true or false; string is a JSON string.
  • enumeration is the name of the enum as a string; bits is a space-separated string of the names of the bits that are set; binary is a base64 string.
  • leafref follows the type of the leaf it points to.
  • identityref is the identity name as a string, namespace-qualified when the identity is defined in another module, as in iana-if-type:ethernetCsmacd.
  • empty is [null], an array holding a single null. This was chosen over plain null because many programming languages treat a null member as absent.
  • union takes the value of any member type, and the JSON type information MUST be taken into account when validating.
  • instance-identifier is a string like the XML form, with the leftmost node always qualified and later nodes qualified only when their module differs from the parent's.

The union rule means JSON can be stricter than XML. For a union of uint16 and string, the XML value 13.5 is accepted as a string, but the JSON number 13.5 is an error. The JSON string "1" is read as a string.
sections.eli5: Each kind of answer has a fixed way to be written, like numbers going in number boxes and words going in word boxes. Very big numbers are written as words so they do not get squished.

sections.title: I-JSON Compliance
sections.content:
I-JSON (RFC 7493) is a restricted profile of JSON meant to keep interoperability high whatever encoder or decoder is used. This encoding follows its requirements and recommendations as closely as possible. It guarantees UTF-8, unique member names within one object, no reliance on member order, and reliable exchange of every number type YANG supports. The last point is why the 64-bit and decimal types are strings, following I-JSON's advice for numbers outside the IEEE 754-2008 double-precision range.

There is one deviation. I-JSON recommends base64url for binary data, but this document keeps ordinary base64 to remain compatible with the XML encoding.

With the exception of anyxml and schema-less anydata nodes, a JSON-encoded tree can be mapped to the XML encoding and back. Such conversions require the YANG model to be available.
sections.eli5: There is a set of strict house rules for JSON so every program reads it the same way. This RFC follows nearly all of them and breaks only one, to stay friendly with the older XML way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This is only an alternative encoding, so it adds no new security issues beyond those in Section 17 of RFC 7950. It defines no mechanism for signing or encrypting data. Normally the management protocol in use, such as NETCONF or RESTCONF, provides data security and integrity. Otherwise external mechanisms such as PKCS #7 or JOSE need to be considered.

JSON processing differs from XML, so parsers may suffer different vulnerabilities. To limit that risk, receiving software SHOULD reject all messages that do not comply with these rules and reply with an appropriate error message.
sections.eli5: This RFC only changes how the settings are written, not how they are kept safe. The tool that carries them must lock them up, and a receiver should refuse anything written wrongly.
